extracted.intended_audience: novelists, creative writers, critics and students of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and handling narrative method (dramatic vs pictorial), point of view, preparation and climax in long fiction, with examples from Balzac and Tolstoy illustrating when to show, when to tell, and how to prepare effects. Useful for writers planning structure and voice for novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve the climax in early pictorial description
rubrics_metrics.description: Lay up the material for the climax in the opening picture so that the climax can use that reserve of effect when it comes: "The climax of the story, as in Grandet, is laid up betimes in the descriptive picture."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build a rich, detailed initial scene (house, possessions, social world) that can later be denuded or destroyed to register the hero's ruin; Balzac's treatment of Claes and the house in La Recherche de l'Absolu shows how the disappearance of treasures renews and heightens the effect rather than diminishes it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax should complete and add the touch that makes the book whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax's task is to complete and add the final touch that makes the book organic: "The climax ought to complete, to add the touch that makes the book whole and organic; that is its task, and that only."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relieve the climax of unnecessary burdens by dealing with anything that can be handled earlier. Let the climax be free to do only what is necessary, unencumbered by newly introduced material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of preparation — don't betray the art of preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparation should be unrecognizable until it attains its end: "The art of preparation is no art if it betrays itself at the outset, calling attention to its purpose."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipattern: heavy-handed foreshadowing or explicit signaling of later effects. Instead, create reserves and hints subtly so the reader discovers the payoff without feeling manipulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent emotional change as slow, temporal development not a sudden stroke
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain effects (disappointment, ruin) are pictorial and need time: "The worst kind of disappointment does not happen like that, falling as a stroke; it steals into a life and spreads imperceptibly."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the subject demands it, depict the gradual accrual of change (a 'slow chill') rather than a single sensational reveal. Use cumulative, incremental incidents to achieve believable emotional decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the subject dictate the method
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of method must follow the subject: "The subject dictates the method."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide between pictorial/retrospective narration and strict scenic/dramatic presentation depending on whether the story needs panoramic survey, interior reflection, or immediate action. Do not force a congenial method on an incompatible subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic (scenic) form: limits and suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: A purely dramatic story is strictly scenic: one occasion or episode follows another without generalization; it is limited to what ear and eye can perceive and admits no private minds directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rigid dramatization where the subject 'will tell itself' in action and where thoughts can be transmuted into action. Expect sacrifices: you lose direct interior access and panoramic survey, but gain compactness and objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial/retrospective form requires a narrator or vantage point
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictorial books involve a point of view which is not the reader's and often require an authorial or internal narrator to gather experience and compose the vision: "In a pictorial book the principle of the structure involves a point of view which is not the reader's."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the story spans time, needs generalization, or treats growth of character/soul, use a reflective narrator (omniscient author or a man in the book) to shape the impression and supply panoramic context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use shifts of point of view to dramatize and give direct sight
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress toward dramatization can be achieved by shifting point of view so the reader sees the action while it is passing rather than as a report: "The spectator... is now himself to be placed at the angle of vision... a direct sight of the matter itself, while it is passing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ purposeful POV shifts (narrator -> spokesperson -> immediate scene) to let the reader witness events directly when that strengthens the drama, while retaining other points of view where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize the author's presence by setting up a spokesman
rubrics_metrics.description: One way to disguise the author's voice and contain authority is to dramatize the author via a spokesman in the book: "If the story-teller is in the book himself, the author is dramatized; his presence is disguised in the voice of his spokesman."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you want to avoid an overt authorial intrusion but need an organizing consciousness, create a credible in-world narrator/spokesman whose authority carries the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show consciousness in the moment rather than report it after the fact
rubrics_metrics.description: If the narrator is himself the subject, seeing him 'while his mind is actually at work' is better than an after-the-fact account: "Far better it would be to see him while his mind is actually at work... The matter would then be objective and visible to the reader."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer scenes that render thought and feeling as they occur (interior immediacy) when the story hinges on the character's consciousness; avoid mere retrospective summarizing that reduces immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condense and tightly pack an initial situation when the action must begin quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: When a story's turning-point must be reached without delay (Anna Karenina example), the opening situation must be tightly packed to convey enough of character and context: "If, therefore, the situation is to be really made and constituted, the space it may cover must be tightly packed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you must launch into high-stakes action early, use concentrated, condensed exposition or summary to furnish the reader with the necessary background quickly; otherwise the protagonist's choices will feel arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: For characters lacking inner resonance, prefer outside/observer treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Some characters are better treated from the outside because they 'lack the poetry, the inner resonance' for sympathetic interior rendering: "Eugénie has not the stuff of character... It is much better to look at it from outside, as Balzac does..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a character is essentially simple or passive, adopt an external, pictorial viewpoint rather than attempting deep psychological interiorization that the material doesn't support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build rich material so destruction or loss yields renewed effect
rubrics_metrics.description: By creating a fully furnished world (architecture, portraits, treasures), the progressive destruction of that world renews and increases the story's force rather than weakening repeated blows: "He has created so much that there is plenty to destroy; only at last... is the wreck complete."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in detailed, tangible objects and settings early so that their gradual loss can visibly manifest the protagonist's moral, social or financial decline; repetition of loss then becomes cumulatively powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exposing the method at the outset — preparation must be unobtrusive
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparation 'must evade detection at the moment' and must not call attention to itself: "By definition it is unrecognizable until it attains its end; it is the art of rendering an impression that is found to have been made, later on."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep foreshadowing and preparatory details subtle. The reader should feel the payoff as discovery rather than feeling the earlier pages were merely 'setting up' the later effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repetition with increasing intensity when the subject is a fixed idea or obsession
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject is the growth of a fixed idea (La Recherche de l'Absolu), the book must reiterate one effect with growing intensity rather than vary incident: "There can be no development through any variety of incident; it is the same suspense and the same shock, again and again, constantly more disastrous than before."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For narratives of obsession or progressive ruin, structure recurring episodes that escalate the stakes and intensity rather than diversifying incident; each repetition should reveal more and deepen the consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small vivid scenes as enrichment to make characters full and ready for climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Brief, luminous glimpses ('half-page' scenes) add eloquent memory and enrich a character so they become 'a complete Being, intimately understood, ready for the climax': Tolstoy's use of many small scenes creates this effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scatter concise, vivid episodes that reveal character through detail; these do not divert but speed the story by enlarging the reader's understanding of the people involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of method-induced failures: match scope and method
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer may trust a congenial method too far and thereby mis-handle a subject (Tolstoy's scenic plan failing to prepare Anna's life): "The method of the book, in short, does not arise out of the subject; in treating it Tolstoy simply used the method that was congenial to him, without regarding the story that he had to tell."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether your habitual or preferred technique serves this specific story's demands. If the method conflicts with the subject (e.g., scenic method for a tale needing panoramic preparation), reconsider method or adapt technique.
